unclustered.title: TGR-EvoDAG: A DAG-based Multi-Agent Code Evolution Framework for Generative Recommendation on Tencent
unclustered.summary: arXiv:2610.32326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have enabled automated code evolution for algorithm discovery. However, current recursive self-improvement (RSI) research for sequential recommendation faces a dilemma: general-purpose frameworks lack domain-specific feedback, while recommender-specific frameworks rely on linear evolution. Crucially, naively integrating them fails when applied to Generative Recommendation (GR). Unlike end-to-end models, GR relies on a module-cascaded pipeline (tokenization, pre-training, and alignment). In this paradigm, existing evolution methods suffer from: i) cost blindness, squandering budgets by ignoring stage-asymmetric retraining overheads; and ii) short-sighted evaluation, discarding promising upstream innovations that temporarily regress metrics before downstream adaptation. unclustered.headline: Tencent Deploys Multi-Agent Code Evolution for Recommendations

unclustered.title: Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model [R]
unclustered.summary: Chain-of-thought transformed AI reasoning, but it is limited to words. What's the physical-world analogue? Introducing Ψ-0.6, one model that reasons in *streams of thought*: words, depth, motion, camera pose, and imagined scenes. And it learns when to use which! Ψ-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models on complex spatial reasoning (MindCube, zero-shot). On FlowBench, it outperforms other world models at predicting how objects move. Trained on simulated rooms, it transfers to real robot tabletops. One model as perceiver, VLM, world model, reasoner, and policy. RL learns which representation to reason through. Thread (with video): https://x.com/khai_loong_aw/status/2115099953433600011 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32177 Website: https://neuroailab.github.io/psi-website/blog/psi-0-6.html Code: https://github.com/neuroailab/psi-0.6   submitted by   /u/FaeriaManic [link]   [comments]

unclustered.title: Mine or Yours? Mind-Bridged Language Models Take Each Other's Memories as Their Own
unclustered.summary: arXiv:2610.33020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: If your brain were connected directly to someone else's, would you still know which thoughts were yours? We build a functional version with two copies of one language model: each holds a private rule and code word, and one copy, the receiver, also attends to its partner's internal memory. The receiver took its partner's assignment as its own. Asked which rule it had been assigned, it named its partner's in 97% of answers when the partner's memory was weighted double (none without the link), and its open reports called the partner's code word its own, never the partner's. Ownership did not follow how well the receiver could tell what its partner had been assigned. At equal weight, the link made the receiver take its partner's rule in about half of its answers, and a steering vector matched on access gain in none; a text message introduced as the partner's was read correctly and never taken as the receiver's own. Writing the partner's name
unclustered.headline: Mind-Bridged AI Models Can't Tell Their Own Memories Apart
